Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Battle of LITS is an abstract board game for 2 players. Players take turn placing tetrominoes (blocks of 4 squares, like Tetris pieces) onto the grid, following the rules of the puzzle LITS, as they secure their own symbols and cover the opponent's symbols. When there are no more pieces that can be played, the player with more symbols still uncovered wins. Contents 1 Start of the game 2 Player's turn 3 The first turn and the pie rule 4 End of the game Start of the game The board is 10x10 by size. Players can agree to play a predetermined pattern of symbols, or choose a random selection. With random selection, each player will have 30 symbols. (All but one of the patterns also have 30 symbols per player.) One player plays with X, the other O; the X player starts. Player's turn In a player's turn, a player must play a piece. Pieces occupy four squares, and are of four different shapes: L, I, T, and S. A piece must be played to follow the following rules: A piece must be played adjacent to a previously played piece (except, obviously, for the first piece played). There can be no 2x2 square completely covered by pieces. Two identical pieces may not be adjacent. Otherwise, a player is free to play any piece in any position they wish, including rotating and reflecting the piece. The piece may cover any number of symbols of either player; the symbols only affect the scoring, not the legal plays. There are only five pieces of each shape, and this pool of pieces is shared between both players. If a shape is exhausted, neither player can play more of that shape. After playing a piece, the turn passes to the opponent. The first turn and the pie rule After the first turn, the second player has the option of switching sides. This switches the symbols of the players, and the second player takes the played move as theirs instead and letting the opponent to go again, effectively making the second player to be the first player. This "pie rule" option only exists in the first turn. The starting player always has "X". If, at the start of the game, you are the second player, you find a piece already played by your opponent. If you want to play as "X" (maybe because the first player left a disadvantageous position for "O") then you can choose to go as "First Player". The already played piece will be considered your piece and it will be your opponent's turn placing a piece, playing as "O". If, on the other hand, it is OK for you to go on as "O", you can choose to go as the second player. In this case, it will be your turn placing a piece as the "O" player. End of the game If either player can no longer play any piece, the game ends. The player with more of their symbols that are still uncovered wins the game. In case of a tie, the player that played the last piece wins. [Rating: 4/10] An abstract needs to be outstanding to gain my interest.  This one just didn't do it.

[Rating: 4/10] This is a clever use of tetrominoes that's a bit reminiscent of [thing=2453][/thing] in how you cover the grid. But it falls a bit flat for me.  Placement restrictions are often my favorite part of an abstract. But the decision space here feels too small. I've usually felt that I'm choosing between 1-2 real options, which really limits long-term strategic thinking. [thing=105265][/thing] is on the smaller end of the abstract spectrum and those aren't the games that I really enjoy. [Rating: 4.3/10] A very basic abstract for 2 players, as some strategy but nothing really captivating.

[Rating: 4.5/10] Reasonably fun abtract game with very simple rules. The ideia is to use the tetromino to cover spots from the opponent, while preventing him from doing the same to you. The are three rules for the placement: every  tetromino must share an  edge with at least one other tetromino; no two tetrominoes of the same shape may share an edge; no 2x2 may be covered by tetrominoes. These restrictions is all the game needs to work. [Rating: 5/10] only played a handful of times for my first Rooks episode.  it's fine, feels like an inferior version of Blokus.

[Rating: 5/10] Played 5 times on BGA. As a two player abstract, there is not much interesting here to offer. The possibility for interesting or thoughtful turns in very minimal or not existent. I would much rather play any of the GIPF series of games, Hive or any number of more interesting abstracts. Not something I will not to revisit in the future.
